newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss Nat'l Bank scoffs at talk it must buy gold.
newsitem.headline: Swiss Nat'l Bank scoffs at talk it must buy gold.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) dismissed as "pure speculation" a suggestion it might have to buy more gold to ensure it respects a government decree that its gold reserves cover at least 40 percent of banknotes in circulation.

The central bank is not planning any imminent changes to the way it handles its gold reserves, spokesman Werner Abegg said, reiterating that the question will only arise once Switzerland reforms its constitution, probably years from now.

SBC Warburg pointed out in a comment for the Finanz und Wirtschaft newspaper that SNB gold reserves covered only around 42 percent of notes in circulation at the moment and that this could dip below 40 percent this month on seasonal factors.
The amount of banknotes traditionally rises during the holiday shopping period. The 40-percent floor could also be broken for good sometime next year, SBC Warburg said.
SBC Warburg said there were three theoretical solutions.
The SNB could tighten monetary policy, but that was unlikely given the weak Swiss economy.

Another solution could be for the government to let the SNB buy more gold by changing the decree that mandates the central bank may only buy or sell gold at a price within 1.5 percent of the fixed gold parity of 4,595.74 Swiss francs per kilogram.

Finally, the government could boost the parity price to be more in line with market prices. SBC Warburg said that was the most likely scenario even though it would force the SNB to pay out its higher net profit to the federal and cantonal governments.
Abegg told Reuters the problem was not a pressing one and that no changes were imminent.

"This is pure speculation what they are writing. This is just a catalogue of possibilities but nothing that is any way being considered at the moment," he said, adding the SNB itself has frequently discussed such options in the past.
He also said the current situation was nothing new.

"That is always like this at the end of the year. The 40 percent is an average measure for the whole year and whenever banknotes in circulation rise, as is the case toward the end of the year, the coverage of gold is not always guaranteed on individual days. That is a development that has been going on for years," he said.
The issue will finally be decided when the lengthy process of constitutional reform, which must snake its way through the legislative system and be approved in a referendum, wraps up.
This could be followed by changes to the National Bank law that would allow more effective management of SNB gold reserves, which are now governed by "outdated" rules, he said.
"I would not say they are no longer being adhered to, but at least they have been overtaken by reality," he said.
